objectives: Prepare a slide of onion cells stained with iodine
Use a light microscope to focus on cells, starting at low power
Draw onion cells and calculate the length of one cell

questions.q: What type of cell has no nucleus?
questions.a: A prokaryotic cell (for example a bacterium).

questions.q: Where is the genetic material in a bacterial cell?
questions.a: A single loop of DNA free in the cytoplasm (not in a nucleus).
Small rings of DNA in a bacterial cell that carry extra genes.

questions.q: Name two structures found in both a bacterial cell and a plant cell.
questions.a: Any two from: cell wall, cell membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes.

questions.q: Which is bigger, a bacterial cell or a plant cell? Roughly how big is a bacterium?
questions.a: A plant cell is bigger. A bacterium is about 1 to 5 micrometres (µm) long.

questions.q: What does a flagellum do for a bacterium?
questions.a: It spins like a tail to help the bacterium move.

engage.hook: The skin inside an onion is only one cell thick. How many onion cells do you think fit side by side across 1 mm?
engage.content: Onion skin cells are roughly 0.2 to 0.3 mm long, so only about 3 to 5 of them fit across 1 mm. Today you will measure one yourself.

learn.heading: Parts of the light microscope

items: Eyepiece: the lens you look through (×10).
Objective lenses: low, medium and high power.
Light or mirror: makes the image brighter.
Stage and clips: hold the slide still.
Coarse focus first, fine focus last.

learn.imageDescription: labelled diagram of a light microscope

learn.heading: Focusing in the right order

steps.label: Lowest power objective in place
steps.note: Turn the nosepiece until it clicks

steps.label: Slide on the stage
steps.note: Hold it still with the clips

steps.label: Look from the side
steps.note: Bring the lens close to the slide without touching it

steps.label: Look through the eyepiece
steps.note: Turn the coarse focus to move the lens away until the cells appear

steps.label: Higher power
steps.note: Switch objective, then use only the fine focus

learn.heading: Biological drawings

items: Use a sharp pencil and single clear lines.
Draw large, at least half a page.
Label with ruled lines that do not cross.
Draw cells you did not see.

learn.imageDescription: wrong and correct biological drawings of cells side by side

learn.heading: Working out the length of one cell
learn.equation: length of one cell = length of field of view ÷ number of cells across

components.name: How far you can see across, measured with the perspex ruler
Count the cells in a line across the field of view

learn.example: The field of view is 1.5 mm across and 6 cells fit across it. 1.5 mm = 1500 µm, so one cell = 1500 ÷ 6 = 250 µm.
learn.imageDescription: labelled biological drawing of onion epidermal cells at x100 magnification

build.q: Which part would you adjust to make the image brighter?
build.explanation: The light or mirror controls how much light passes up through the slide.

build.q: Which part would you adjust to make a blurry image clear?
build.explanation: The focus knobs move the lens to make the image sharp: coarse first, then fine.

build.q: The eyepiece magnifies ×10 and the objective lens magnifies ×40. What is the total magnification?
build.explanation: Multiply them: 10 × 40 = 400. Adding them (50) is the common mistake.

build.q: Why do you look from the side while moving the objective lens towards the slide?
options: So the lens does not hit and crack the slide
build.explanation: From the side you can stop just before the lens touches the slide.

build.q: Why do we add iodine to the onion cells?
options: To stain the cells so the nucleus and walls show up
build.explanation: Onion cells are almost see-through. Iodine stains them so the structures are visible.

build.q: Why is the coverslip lowered at an angle using forceps?
options: To stop air bubbles getting trapped
So it does not get wet
build.explanation: Lowering one edge first pushes the air out, so bubbles do not hide the cells.

build.title: Looking at onion cells
build.intro: Make a slide of onion skin stained with iodine, find the cells at low power, then draw them and work out the length of one cell.
equipment: piece of onion (cut by the teacher)
iodine solution in a dropping bottle
steps: Put one drop of water in the middle of the slide.
Peel a thin layer of skin from the inside of the onion piece and lay it flat in the water with forceps.
Add two drops of iodine on top of the onion skin.
Lower the coverslip at an angle with the forceps. Dab away extra liquid with paper towel.
Clip the slide on the stage. Start with the lowest power objective and look from the side as you bring the lens close.
Look through the eyepiece and focus with the coarse knob, then the fine knob. Switch to ×100 and refocus with the fine knob.
Draw a few cells, label them and write the magnification under your drawing.
Put the perspex ruler on the stage, measure the field of view, count the cells across it and work out the length of one cell.
build.warning: Eye protection on. Iodine is harmful: wash it off your skin. Carry microscopes with two hands. Report broken slides.
build.imageDescription: model biological drawing of onion epidermal cells labelled cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus, magnification x100

questions.q: Why must the layer of onion skin be very thin?
questions.a: So light can pass through it and you see single cells, not a dark blur of layers.

questions.q: Why are there no chloroplasts in the onion cells?
questions.a: The onion bulb grows underground with no light, so its cells do not photosynthesise.

developing.q: Name the part of the microscope you turn to bring the image into focus.
developing.a: The focus knob (coarse focus first, then fine focus).

developing.q: Why is iodine added to the onion cells?
developing.a: It stains the cells so the nucleus and cell wall can be seen.

developing.q: Name three structures you can see in an onion cell stained with iodine.
developing.a: Any three from: cell wall, nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane.

reaching.q: The eyepiece lens is ×10 and the objective lens is ×10. What is the total magnification?
The field of view is 2 mm across and 8 onion cells fit across it. Calculate the length of one cell in micrometres.
reaching.given: field of view = 2 mm, 8 cells across
reaching.equation: length of one cell = length of field of view ÷ number of cells

reaching.q: Explain why you should always start with the lowest power objective lens.
reaching.a: It shows the largest area, so the cells are easier to find and focus, and the lens is further from the slide so it is less likely to hit it.

mastering.q: Describe how to prepare a slide of onion cells and view them clearly with a light microscope. (6 marks)
mastering.a: Put a drop of water on a slide. Peel a thin layer of onion skin and lay it flat in the water with forceps. Add iodine to stain it. Lower a coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles. Put the slide on the stage, use the lowest power objective and bring the lens close while looking from the side. Focus with the coarse then fine knob, then move to a higher power and refocus with the fine knob.
indicativeContent: Put a drop of water on a clean slide
Peel a thin layer of onion skin and lay it flat with forceps
Lower the coverslip at an angle to avoid air bubbles
Start with the lowest power objective, bringing the lens close while looking from the side
Focus with the coarse then fine knob, then switch to higher power and use only the fine knob

mastering.q: A student's drawing of onion cells is shaded in and has no title. Give two improvements and explain why a scale bar is useful.
mastering.a: Use clear single lines with no shading; add a title and the magnification. A scale bar shows the real size of the cells whatever size the drawing is printed.

mastering.q: Compare an onion cell with a bacterial cell. Give three differences.
mastering.a: The onion cell has a nucleus, the bacterium does not; the bacterium has its DNA as a loop free in the cytoplasm and may have plasmids; the onion cell is much bigger (about 250 µm compared with 1 to 5 µm).
